cells.verb: working steadily, mostly alone, at something until it lives in your hands
cells.place: in how you're close to people — how you feel with them, not just about them
cells.ask: When one of your old rules for how to be close stops holding, let it fall and don't rebuild it — solitude that leaves you nearer to people, and refining that comes from wanting to grow rather than from fear of getting it wrong.
cells.core:
You're practicing how to be with people, and it's working. The time you spend alone doesn't take you away from anyone — you come back from it closer, with more to offer. You keep refining how you show up, and it's the kind of refining that comes from wanting to be better with someone, not from being afraid you aren't.

That steadiness is quietly making room for something. At some point one of the ways you've always done closeness will turn out to be a rule you no longer need. You'll know it when you see it. You don't have to fight for it to go — you could just let it fall, and not build another one in its place.
cells.sheetLine: You practice closeness the way you'd practice anything, and it's making you better at it.

cells.tense: Future — bracing at a version of this you can't write in yet.
cells.verb: refining how you show up for people past the point anyone asked
cells.place: in how you're close to people — how you feel with them, not just about them
cells.ask: Pick one thing about how you love someone and call it finished — put it down as done, not abandoned — and see what comes back: time alone that connects you instead of walling you off, refining that serves the closeness rather than the fear of losing it.
cells.core:
You're perfecting how you care for people, and the perfecting has started to replace the caring. Somewhere ahead is a version of you who's finally gotten it right, and you're working toward that one instead of being with the person in front of you now. The time alone that used to help has stopped feeling like a choice; it feels required. And underneath there's a question you'd rather not look at — what happens if you stop.

The way through here isn't more effort. It's letting something be done. Not quitting it — finishing it. Deciding that one piece of how you show up is already enough and setting it down as complete.
cells.sheetLine: You're perfecting how you care instead of caring.

cells.tense: Past — still standing at a door that's already behind you.
cells.verb: not able to keep at the steady, repeated work of it
cells.place: in how you're close to people — how you feel with them, not just about them
cells.ask: Don't push yourself to practice closeness harder. Instead, take one exchange — where you've been giving more than comes back, or taking more than you give — and make it fair this week; the capacity to keep at it starts to return on its own: time alone that connects, refinement that comes from growth and not from dread.
cells.core:
Working steadily at how you're close to someone has come to feel dangerous, and so you don't sustain it. You start and then you stop. Something back there taught you that putting repeated, patient effort into feeling with people doesn't end well, and that room is still giving you instructions. I don't know what the room was. You do.

The mistake here would be to try harder at the exact thing that feels unsafe. There's another way in. The part of you that can tell when an exchange is fair — what you give, what you get — is sitting right alongside this one, and feeding it pulls the current through. Settle even one lopsided account and the practicing stops feeling like walking into fire.
cells.sheetLine: You start the work of being close and can't keep at it.

cells.tense: Disowned present — pen down in a room you're already writing.
cells.verb: already practicing how to be with people, every day
cells.place: in how you're close to people — how you feel with them, not just about them
cells.ask: The next time being with someone goes well, say out loud that you don't know how it works yet, and let it stay unclear a while — take only the next step with them without a map — and what returns is your own practice, owned: time alone that connects, refining that serves growth instead of hiding behind 'it just comes naturally'.
cells.core:
You're good with people and you'd tell anyone it just comes naturally. It doesn't. You practice it — in the way you listen, in the things you've quietly stopped doing because they didn't land, in the time alone where you turn conversations over — and it's so woven into how you move that you don't see it as work. Or you're refusing to practice something, and calling that natural too.

Either way the work is yours and you've handed the credit to luck. The way back isn't to catalogue your method. It's simpler than that: admit you don't know how you do this, and stay in that not-knowing long enough to get curious about it, one next step at a time. Owning a skill starts with wondering how you got it.
cells.sheetLine: You practice this every day and call it a gift.

flags.detail: "for years" — a cell knows no one's past
